---
order: 5
unit: civics
title: Three levels of government
node: [AC9HS6K07 n1, AC9HS6K07 n4, AC9HS6K06 n1]
summary: "Australia has three levels of government, each looking after different things. Local councils look after things like rubbish, parks and local roads. State and territory governments look after things like schools, hospitals and police. The federal (Australian) government looks after things that affect the whole country, like money, defence and immigration. In the ACT, the ACT Government does both the state and the local jobs."
language: science
shape: primer
assumes: [AC9HS6K07 n3, AC9HS6K01]
hook: "A pothole on your street, a new school and the money in your pocket. Is one government in charge of all three?"
---
Australia has **three levels of government**. Each one looks after different things, and each has its own elected representatives.

- **Local councils** look after things in your local area: rubbish and recycling, parks and sports fields, local roads, libraries and pet control.
- **State and territory governments** look after things across a state or territory: schools, hospitals, police and public transport.
- **The federal government** (the Australian Government) looks after things that affect the whole country: money, defence, immigration, and post and the internet.

Each level has people you elect, and each can make laws for its own jobs. A council makes local laws, such as rules for dogs in parks. A state parliament makes laws for the state, such as road rules. The federal Parliament makes laws for the whole country.

Three kinds of institution run through the system. **Parliaments** make laws. **Courts** decide what the law means when people disagree. And the **King**, represented by the Governor-General (and a Governor in each state), signs laws passed by Parliament.

**If you live in Canberra:** the ACT has no local councils. The ACT Government does both the state jobs and the local jobs.

Wattle Creek, where these examples happen, is a made-up town.

## Think first

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students think one government runs everything."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A pothole appears on a street in Wattle Creek. Which level of government usually fixes it?"
  options: ["The local council", "The federal government", "The state government", "The Prime Minister"]
  actual: "The local council. Local roads are a council job. Highways and main roads are usually looked after by the state."
```

## Try: who looks after it?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting everyday services into the three levels shows that each level has its own jobs."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Which level of government looks after each one?"
  options: ["Local council", "State or territory", "Federal"]
  items:
    - ["Emptying the bins", "Local council", "Rubbish and recycling are council jobs."]
    - ["Running the town's park", "Local council", "Parks and sports fields are council jobs."]
    - ["Running public hospitals", "State or territory", "Hospitals are a state or territory job."]
    - ["Running public schools", "State or territory", "Public schools are run by the state or territory."]
    - ["Making Australia's money", "Federal", "Money is a federal job, the same for the whole country."]
    - ["Defending the country", "Federal", "Defence is a federal job."]
```

## The idea: each level has its own jobs

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Seeing Nib blame the Prime Minister for a pothole shows why it matters to know which level does what."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Click the first line where Nib goes wrong."
      answer: 3
      fault: logic
      misconception: one-government-does-everything
      explain: "Line 3: the Prime Minister leads the federal government, which doesn't fix local streets. The local council does."
    smaller:
      check: { type: question, q: "Who empties the bins in Wattle Creek?", options: ["The local council", "The federal government", "The state government"], answer: 0, explain: "Bins are a local council job.", feedback: [null, "The federal government looks after the whole country, like money and defence, not your street's bins.", "States run schools, hospitals and police. Bins are closer to home."] }
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why does Australia have three levels of government?"
      options:
        - "So town, state and country matters each get looked after"
        - "So the federal government can run every council's work"
        - "So one level makes all the laws for the other two"
        - "So a state can overrule the federal government"
      answer: 0
      feedback:
        - null
        - "Councils make their own decisions about local jobs. The federal government doesn't run them."
        - "Each level makes laws for its own jobs: councils, states and the federal Parliament."
        - "When a state law and a federal law clash, the federal law wins. That comes up in Year 7."
      explain: "Some things matter mostly to a town, some to a state, and some to the whole country."
```

## Vary: who does what?

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Matching the three institutions to their jobs gives the Year 7 course its starting words."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each part of the system to its job."
  pairs:
    - ["A parliament", "Makes laws"]
    - ["A court", "Decides what the law means when people disagree"]
    - ["The Governor-General", "Represents the King and signs laws passed by Parliament"]
    - ["A local council", "Makes local laws, such as rules for dogs in parks"]
```

## Check: before you move on

```step
stage: practise
insight: "One more sort on a new day in the made-up town."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "A day in Wattle Creek. Which level looks after each one?"
  options: ["Local council", "State or territory", "Federal"]
  items:
    - ["The library where you borrow a book", "Local council", "Local libraries are usually run by councils."]
    - ["The police officer at the school crossing", "State or territory", "Police are a state or territory job."]
    - ["Deciding who can move to Australia", "Federal", "Immigration is a federal job."]
```

## Evaluate

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name the three levels of government and give an example of what each one looks after." }
```

## Make: your own

```step
stage: make
insight: "Naming a service from each level in their own area makes the idea the student's own."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I wrote one thing each level of government looks after where I live (or, in Canberra, which ones the ACT Government does). A partner read it and gave feedback." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students name Australia's three levels of government (local, state or
  territory, federal) and sort everyday services by which level looks after
  them. In the ACT, the ACT Government does both state and local jobs.
learning: name the three levels of government and give an example of what each
  looks after
time: 20
timing: Think first and Try 6 min · The idea 6 min · Vary and Check 5 min · Make 5 min.
goals:
  - I can say what a parliament, a court and the Governor-General do.
  - I can name the three levels of government.
  - I can give an example of what each level looks after.
struggle: Students think one government, often 'the Prime Minister', runs
  everything. Ask 'Is this a matter for a town, a state or the whole country?'
before: >
  This is a Year 6 catch-up for AC9HS6K07 (with AC9HS6K06 n1). Year 7 *The
  Constitution - rules for the rule-makers* and *One country, several
  governments* build on it.


  Responsibilities follow the Parliamentary Education Office's summary. Some are
  shared or blurred (health and education are shared between federal and state;
  main roads are state, local roads are council), so the sorts use clear
  examples only. Councils are set up by state laws, not by the Constitution;
  that comes up in Year 7 federation.


  ACT: the ACT has no local councils; the ACT Government and Legislative
  Assembly do both territory and local jobs (ACT Legislative Assembly). Canberra
  students should know their bins, parks and libraries are run by the ACT
  Government. The Make step lets them say so.


  K06 n1 (parliaments, courts, the monarch and the Governor-General) is one
  match step only; Year 7 *The Constitution* and *Power shared and checked* go
  further. K07 n3 (where new laws come from) and Federation (K01) are left to
  Year 6 class.


  Wattle Creek is made up.
running:
  - "Think first: take a show of hands. Many will pick the Prime Minister or the
    state."
  - "Try: if you're in Canberra, ask who empties the bins here."
stuck:
  - see: A student says the Prime Minister runs everything.
    ask: Is a pothole a matter for the whole country?
    fix: Local matters go to the council; state matters to the state; national
      matters to the federal government.
stretch: Find one thing two levels of government share, such as health.
support: "Three columns on the board: TOWN, STATE, COUNTRY."
leads: >
  Next in Year 7: The Constitution - rules for the rule-makers, and One country,
  several governments.
exit:
  q: Name the three levels of government and one thing each looks after.
  a: Local council (bins), state or territory (schools), federal (money).
explain: >
  Australia has **three levels of government**: **local councils** (bins, parks,
  local roads), **state and territory governments** (schools, hospitals, police)
  and the **federal government** (money, defence, immigration). In the ACT, the
  ACT Government does both state and local jobs.
sources:
  - title: The responsibilities of the three levels of government (Parliamentary
      Education Office)
    url: https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/three-levels-of-government/the-responsibilities-of-the-three-levels-of-government
    checked: 2026-11-01
  - title: Levels of government in the ACT (ACT Legislative Assembly)
    url: https://www.parliament.act.gov.au/visit-and-learn/learn/resources/fs/levels-of-gov
    checked: 2026-11-01
class:
  activities:
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Town, state or country?
      minutes: 3
      do: Call out services (bins, hospitals, money). The class points to TOWN, STATE
        or COUNTRY on the board.
```
